title: The many faces of Krátos
description: From Greek to Unicode: why Krátos is more than a domain name.
author: PuniCodex Team
body:
# The many faces of Krátos

No important name has only one face. **Krátos** appears as ​a figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and — most recently — a Unicode domain. This post looks at each face in ‌turn: the name and its roots, the Greek original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the symbols and sanctuaries, the cross-cultural afterlife, and the engineering that lets the restored spelling resolve in ‌a browser. Taken together, those faces explain why *kratos* was never going to be enough — and why the restored form is worth a domain of its own.

## At a Glance

- **Restored ​name:** Krátos
- **ASCII form:** kratos
- **Meaning:** "Strength, power"
- **Domain of influence:** Strength, Power, Sovereignty
- **Pantheon:** Greek
- **Restoration:** Preserves stress
- **Original script:** Κράτος (Greek)
- **Live domain:** krátos.com

## Overview

**Krátos** (*kratos*) — Strength, Power, ​Sovereignty · Strength, power — belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Strength, Power, Sovereignty". The name means "Strength, power".

**Krátos** belongs to the Greek tradition, where ​it is associated with strength, power, sovereignty.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Krátos** and serves its temple at [kratos.com](https://punicodex.com/kratos/). The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather ​than both. The plain ASCII form *kratos* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## ​The Name

The name is attested in Greek as **Κράτος**. Etymologically it means "Strength, power".

The reconstructed proto-form is *kret-* (proto-indo-european, "to be strong"). Greek κράτος 'strength, power, might'; personified as one ‌of the children of the Titan Pallas and Styx.

The ASCII form *kratos* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient ​spelling. The Unicode restoration **Krátos** recovers the stress accent of the original directly in the address bar. The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both.

​The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **k** → **K** — Kappa
- **r** → **r** — Rho
- **a** → **á** — Acute on alpha
- **t** → **t** — Tau
- **o** → **o** — Omicron
- **s** ‌→ **s** — Sigma

The canonical temple for this name is served at **kratos.com**.

## Etymology & Roots

The recorded derivation reads: Greek κράτος 'strength, power, might'; personified as one of the children ​of the Titan Pallas and Styx.

The reconstructed proto-form is **kret-* (proto-indo-european), glossed as "to be strong".

The reconstruction is classed as attested.

## The Original Script

The name is written in Greek ‌as **Κράτος**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *kratos* and the PuniCodex restoration **Krátos** are measured: the restoration preserves its pitch accent of the written form, so ​that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/kratos/** — Greek Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **K** — Initial character ‌of the restored form Krátos.
- **rátos** — Remainder of the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Greek tradition.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'KRATOS' — pronounce the restored ​form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Greek** — Krátos, the restored Unicode form of the name

Krátos is a simpler restoration because ​the Greek form preserves distinctive features that ASCII loses: stress, length, or special characters.

## Mythology

The stories of **Krátos** circulate within the Greek corpus, where the figure embodies strength, power, sovereignty.

### Primary ​Attestation (Sources)

Krátos is attested in the canonical Greek sources as a figure associated with strength, power, sovereignty.

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "Strength, power" and reflects the figure's role ​in the tradition. **Krátos** is the personification of strength or sovereign power in Greek poetry. In Aeschylus's *Prometheus Bound* he is the pitiless agent who compels Hephaestus to bind Prometheus, embodying the ​coercive force that even the craftsman-god cannot refuse. Unlike his brother Bía (Violence), Krátos represents institutionalized, legitimate might. His pairing with Bía in the binding of Prometheus shows that Greek tragedy could ‌personify abstract forces and set them in dialogue with the gods.

### The Children of Styx (Theogony 375–403)

Hesiod gives Krátos his family in the *Theogony* (375–383): the river Styx, daughter of Ocean, ​bore to Pallas four children — **Zelos** (Rivalry), trim-ankled **Níkē** (Victory), **Krátos** (Might), and **Bía** (Force). They are not decorative attendants. When the Titanomachy broke out, Styx was the first of the ‌gods to bring her children over to Zeus's side, and for that loyalty Zeus granted them a rare honor: they live with him forever, 'for he ordained that they should dwell with ​him always and have honor beyond the other gods' (Theogony 383–403). Hyginus (*Fabulae*, preface) repeats the list and calls them *primos in omnibus* — first among all. The myth explains something precise ‌about Greek ideas of rule: victory, rivalry, might, and force are not Zeus's rivals but his household, bound to him by gratitude and oath.

### The Will of Zeus (Prometheus Bound 1–87)

Aeschylus ​stages Krátos in person. At the opening of *Prometheus Bound*, Might and Force — **Krátos and Bía** — drag the defiant Titan to a crag at the world's edge, and Krátos addresses ‌the workman Hephaestus with the play's entire thesis: Zeus is new to power and ruthless; old loyalties count for nothing; 'there is no one free except Zeus' (Prometheus Bound 50–52). Hephaestus pities ​Prometheus and hesitates over the hammer; Krátos has no pity to hesitate with — he only checks that the work is done. Then he leaves the stage, his task complete, and ‌never returns: force has nothing more to say once the chain is set. The drama built the West's first portrait of power as a functionary — efficient, unpersuadable, bored by the suffering ​it administers — and gave the abstraction a mask the audience could boo.

### The Oath of Styx (Theogony 775–806)

Krátos's mother is herself an institution. In the *Theogony* (775–806) Hesiod explains that ​when the gods must swear their most terrible oath, they swear by **Styx**: an Olympian pours her water, and any god who forswears lies breathless for a full year, then serves nine ‌more years exiled from the divine company. Zeus granted her this honor precisely because her children had stood by him in the war — the oath of the gods is, literally, the ‌reward of loyalty. So Krátos descends from the one power in the cosmos that even Zeus must respect: the pledge by which rule itself is guaranteed. The genealogy is a lesson in ‌political theology — might and the binding oath are mother and son, because force that cannot be sworn to is only violence, and an oath that cannot be enforced is only a ​wish.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Krátos concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Restored Name** — The Unicode form Krátos carries ​the original marks of the Greek tradition.
- **Source Script** — Attested in the original script as Κράτος.
- **Domain** — Strength, Power, Sovereignty
- **Etymology** — Strength, power

Krátos is shown as a **muscular, ‌beardless youth** wielding a hammer or club, often beside Hephaistos at the crucifixion of Prometheus. His attributes are bonds, anvil, and the reluctant tools of punishment.

The figure blends personification with the ​aesthetic of the divine craftsman's assistant.

- **The adamantine bonds** — The unbreakable chains Hephaestus forged in ignorance and Krátos fastens without pity (Prometheus Bound)
- **The Scythian crag** — The remote cliff at ​the world's edge where Prometheus is nailed — the geography of force's work
- **Styx, mother** — The underworld river whose oath binds the gods themselves — Krátos is born of the most ‌terrible pledge
- **The house of Zeus** — His only dwelling: the permanent right, granted after the Titanomachy, to sit forever beside the ruler of Olympus

## Epithets & Cult Titles

Krátos is paired ​with **Βία** (*Bia*, Force) and called **κραταιός** (*krataios*, mighty), **καρτερός** (*karteros*, staunch), and **δεσμοφύλαξ** (*desmophylax*, guard of bonds). His name becomes an abstract noun for sovereign power, used of gods, kings, and ​armies.

The absence of cult epithets reflects his near-abstract role as the executive arm of Zeus's will.

## The Homeric Hymns

**Krátos** appears in the opening of **Aeschylus's Prometheus Bound** as the personification ‌of Strength, dragging the Titan to his punishment at Hephaistos's forge. While not the subject of a Homeric Hymn, his speech in the prologue is itself a hymnic assertion of Zeuss ​irresistible power.

The fragmentary *Prometheus Unbound* and Hesiod's **Theogony** name him a son of the Titan Pallas and the river Styx.

## Oracle Sites & Sanctuaries

Krátos had no independent cult or oracle; ‌his presence is felt wherever Zeus's authority is enforced. The **Sicyonian** temple of Zeus had an altar to Kratos and Bia, honouring the powers that underpinned oath and obedience.

He is therefore ​a theological personification rather than a sanctuary god.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Krátos survives in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus is thin but ​unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

Krátos is attested in the textual and iconographic record of the Greek tradition.

Attested in the sources as Κράτος.  Krátos therefore names not raw muscle but the authorized capacity to enforce decree, distinguishing political order from mere ‌violence.

## Across Cultures

Krátos appears within the Greek tradition and has influenced later retellings, artistic depictions, and scholarly study. The Unicode restoration preserves the name's distinctive orthography for contemporary use.

Within the ‌Greek tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[acheron|Achérōn]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], [[adamas|Adámas]], [[aer|Aḗr]], [[aither|Aithḗr]], and [[ananke|Anánkē]].

## Cultural Legacy

Krátos continues to appear in scholarship, art, and popular reception as a significant figure ​of the Greek tradition. Restoring the name in Unicode returns the original marks that ASCII removes. The name survives in modern Greek *kratos* (state) and in English derivatives such as "democracy" and ‌"autocracy."

## A Meditation

Krátos embodies strength, power, sovereignty in the Greek imagination. The name's restoration is not merely cosmetic: it recovers the stress, length, and script that make ‌the figure recognizable in the source tradition.

## The Unicode Restoration

Krátos preserves stress. The ASCII fallback *kratos* still resolves everywhere, but it is the restored form that carries the name's full information. ‌Across the 6 characters of the name, the restoration adjusts 1: 1 mark of stress (á). That is the whole thesis of this temple: the marks are the message.

## Character by Character

‌The journey from *kratos* to **Krátos**, one character at a time:

- **k** → **K** — Kappa
- **r** → **r** — Rho
- **a** → **á** — Acute on alpha
- **t** → **t** ‌— Tau
- **o** → **o** — Omicron
- **s** → **s** — Sigma

## The Domain Name

The restored name is live as a working domain: **krátos.com**, which the DNS carries in punycode form ​as xn--krtos-yqa.com — an ASCII-compatible encoding that lets a non-ASCII name travel the global network without breaking older infrastructure. The visitor sees Krátos; the machines see the encoding. That duality is the ‌engineering compromise on which the entire restoration rests, and it is why a name written the way its own tradition wrote it in Greek can now be typed into any browser on ​earth.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What does Krátos mean?** The traditional ​gloss is "Strength, power."

**Which tradition does Krátos belong to?** Krátos is catalogued in the Greek pantheon of the PuniCodex lexicon.

**What does Krátos preserve that ASCII cannot show?** The form itself ‌answers: Krátos preserves stress — and the marks in the restored spelling are exactly that evidence.

**Is Krátos a working domain?** Yes — krátos.com resolves today and routes to this temple.

**What ​is the punycode for krátos.com?** The DNS encoding is xn--krtos-yqa.com; browsers perform the translation automatically, so visitors only ever see the restored name.

**Can I use Krátos in a normal browser?** Yes. ​The DNS resolves the punycode form automatically, and the type tool on this site converts kratos to Krátos for copying and pasting.

**Where does the scholarly information come from?** The entry is ​built from lexica, inscriptional evidence, and reviewed scholarly sources listed in the Scholarly Edition. Every claim is traceable to a canonical source.

## Typing Krátos

You do not need a special keyboard to ‌use this restoration. The [PuniCodex Type Tool](/type/) converts the ASCII form *kratos* into **Krátos** as you type, and the browser extension offers the same conversion inside any text field. Copy the restored ​form, paste it into the address bar, and the DNS does the rest.

## Why This Restoration Matters

Myth, script, sound, cult, legacy, domain: the faces of Krátos add up to a single ​argument — that a name is a record, and records deserve fidelity. The PuniCodex restoration keeps that record in working order: the temple presents it, the Scholarly Edition footnotes it, the ‌lexicon catalogs it, and the domain makes it addressable. *kratos* will always exist as a fallback. But fallback is not identity. **Krátos** is the name; everything else is a convenience.

## ​A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In **Krátos**, the journey from the ASCII fallback *kratos* to the Unicode form can be read letter by letter, ‌and each letter tells a story. Of the 6 characters, 5 remain unchanged; they anchor the name to its modern shape. The remaining adjustments recover marks the source tradition used to distinguish ​this name from every other word built from the same letters.

The **k** stays as it is — Kappa.

The **r** stays as it is — Rho.

The **a** becomes **á** — ‌Acute on alpha.

The **t** stays as it is — Tau.

The **o** stays as it is — Omicron.

The **s** stays as it is — Sigma.

Together these changes are not ‌decoration. They are the minimum set of marks needed to keep the name legible in its own tradition. Remove them and you still have a string of letters; you no longer have ​the name as it was written.

## Krátos in Its Tradition

**Krátos** does not stand alone. It belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is counted among 279 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. ​Its sphere — Strength, Power, Sovereignty — places it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way ​of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the address bar shows **Krátos**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living ​catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every restored name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between ‌a tradition and a trend. **Krátos** is one such vote.
